passage: With the founders' savings due to go into the account on Friday, Ritu and Tanuja had only one evening left. Ritu wrote on the whiteboard: "It is a year from now and the company is dead. Why?" They did not argue for or against the idea; they just listed reasons. No distribution: nobody knows we exist. One of the two of us wanting a salary again. A slow sales cycle: schools take months to decide. Beside each reason they wrote one small early check: five calls to school principals this week, a frank talk about what each of them needs to live on, and one paid pilot before month three. By ten they were tired but calmer. The list did not make the risk vanish. It gave it edges.

qa.q: What question did Ritu write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Ritu wrote: "It is a year from now and the company is dead. Why?"

qa.q: How did Ritu and Tanuja feel by ten o'clock?
qa.a: They felt tired but calmer, since the list gave the risk edges.

qa.q: What other approach could they use to test the riskiest reason?
qa.a: They could run a cheap experiment on the biggest risk, such as a trial with one school, before spending the savings.

qa.q: How might a school principal see the five calls?
qa.a: A school principal may find the calls a welcome chance to say what a school really needs, or a nuisance if they come at a busy time.

passage:
Before either of them moved a rupee from savings, Afreen made Charu sit on the floor of her Bandra flat with a pad of sticky notes.
"It's March next year. Our company is dead. Why?"
Charu laughed, then didn't. "Nobody found us. We built it and no salon knew it existed."
Afreen wrote: No way to reach customers. "What else?"
"One of us left. Maybe me, if my father's shop needs me."
"And?"
"Salons took six months to decide, and we ran out before they paid."
Three yellow notes on the wall. Afreen said, "Okay. One small check for each, this month." They agreed: get ten salons to a free demo through one beauty-supply distributor; talk honestly about the shop on Sunday; and ask three salon owners how long they usually take to buy software.
Only then did they open their banking apps.

qa.q: What three reasons did they write on the wall?
qa.a: No way to reach customers, one of them leaving, and salons taking six months to decide.
Charu saw the exercise was serious and felt uneasy facing real risks, like possibly having to leave for the father's shop.

qa.q: Which early check seems most urgent, and why?
qa.a: Asking salon owners how long they take to buy, because a slow sale could drain their savings before any payment arrives.

qa.q: How might the shop affect the plan?
qa.a: If the shop needs Charu, the team could lose a partner, which is why they agreed to talk about it honestly on Sunday.

grounding: It shows a team imagining their company dead in a year, listing reasons such as no route to customers, a partner leaving and slow sales, and setting one early check for each.

passage:
"Before we sign the lease and put in our savings," Preeti said, "humour me. It's a year from now. The bakery-supply startup is dead. What killed it?"
Seema put down her chai. "That's morbid."
"It's cheaper than finding out. Go."
"Fine. Bakeries never heard of us. We had no way to reach them."
"Good. Next."
"You got bored and went back to your bank job."
"Ouch. Fair. Next."
"Big hotel kitchens took nine months to approve a new supplier."
"So three ways to die." Preeti wrote them down. "For each one, what can we check before we spend anything?"
"For the first, we visit twenty bakeries this month and see who'd order."
"For me leaving, we sit down every month and I say honestly how I feel."
"For the hotels, we call two chefs and ask how long approvals take."
"Then we sign the lease. Maybe."

qa.q: How long did Seema say hotel kitchens took to approve a supplier?
How did Preeti feel when Seema said "You got bored and went back to your bank job"?
qa.a: It stung a little, hence "Ouch", but Preeti accepted it as a fair risk instead of getting defensive.

qa.q: Why is checking before signing the lease a sensible order?
qa.a: It tests the biggest risks cheaply first, so savings aren't locked into a lease for a business that might fail for a known reason.

qa.q: How does Seema see the exercise at first?
qa.a: Seema finds it morbid, but joins in once Preeti says it's cheaper than finding out.

grounding: It shows two partners imagining their startup dead in a year, naming causes like no route to customers, a partner leaving and slow approvals, and planning an early check for each.
